Method: I instrumented the app with a probe module (src/probe.ts) that walks the live GTK widget tree every 2 s through Gio.Application.getDefault() / Gtk.Application.getWindows() and appends every label it finds to probe/trace.log, plus a file-triggered `button.emit("clicked")` so I could drive the running app without a display. That gave a real oracle for "what is on screen right now" instead of trusting the dev server's own log. 10 `gtkx dev` sessions (probe/dev1.log … probe/dev10.log) plus a run inside a private network namespace (probe/dev-netns.log) to rule out the Vite HMR port.

Sequences exercised, each from a working app, checking the widget tree after every step:
- JSX-only edit (label text): patched in place, state preserved. Correct.
- Adding a useState (hook signature change): clean remount, state reset. Correct per the React Fast Refresh contract.
- Reordering three useState calls: clean remount, no slot-swapped/corrupt state. Correct.
- Editing an event handler (onClicked + 1 -> + 10) then clicking: the new closure runs (count 1 -> 11). No stale handler.
- Syntax error, save, fix: session survives, error names the right file/line with a code frame, recovers on the fix.
- Runtime throw in render, and a throw in useEffect, and a missing import (`<Extra />` used before its import line existed): **kills the whole dev session** (finding 1).
- Deleting an imported file, then editing the importer: clean "Failed to load url ./extra.js … Does the file exist?", app survives. Restoring the file does not replay the failed edit (needs one more save) but that path did report an error, so I did not file it.
- Editing a child module (src/extra.tsx): patched, state preserved.
- 20 saves at 50 ms and 8 two-file "save all" rounds: correct.
- 30 saves at 5 ms, and as few as 2 saves 10 ms apart: **UI left permanently stale** while the log says "Fast Refresh complete" (finding 2).
- Editing gtkx.config.ts (applicationId): supervisor regenerates bindings, restarts the runner, new id takes effect. Correct.
- 10 @gtkx/css style-object edits during a session: no criticals, no leak of the session, app alive.
- SIGTERM to the `gtkx dev` supervisor: graceful, no orphans. SIGKILL to the supervisor: the detached runner exits too via the IPC disconnect handler, no orphans. SIGKILL to the app/runner: the supervisor exits with the signal code (silently, but defensibly).
- Two `gtkx dev` sessions on one project: the second is a silent windowless remote GApplication (finding 3).

Not reached this round: driving the app through @gtkx/mcp (the MCP socket /run/user/1001/gtkx-mcp.sock is a single machine-global socket shared with the other hunters' apps, so I used direct GTK introspection instead and left MCP to the `mcpdrive` persona); adding a dependency to package.json mid-session; editing tsconfig.json mid-session; editing exactly while the window is closing (I could not time it reliably); a module shared between the app and a worker.

All three findings have self-contained scripts under /home/eugenio/gtkx-playground/hotreload-r1/repro/ that build their own project from the template into a fresh /tmp dir; none of them touch bughunt-template or the worktree.

GSettings rejecting an out-of-range write prints a GLib-GIO-WARNING and `useSetting`'s setter swallows it silently, but the schema constraint is enforced exactly as the docs describe and React state stays consistent, so I did not count it.

Scratch area: /home/eugenio/gtkx-playground/lifecycle-r1 (copy of bughunt-template, @gtkx/*@1.0.0). One change was needed to the template before anything ran: its `applicationId` is `com.gtkx.bughunt`, and a stray `node dist/bundle.js` left behind by another agent already owned that name on the session bus, so every launch registered as a remote instance and exited 0 with no window and no message. I changed `gtkx.config.ts` to `com.gtkx.lifecycler1`. Note for other hunters: `.bughunt/run-headless.sh` does NOT kill the app — `wlheadless-run` puts the app in its own session, so `kill -TERM -$pgid` misses it and every 124 run leaks an app plus its weston. I worked around this with my own `cleanup.sh`/`sigtest3.sh` (run the app directly against a compositor I own, so its exit status is observable).

Exercised, per the lifecycle persona:
- Promisified GIO async: resolve, reject on a missing file, GCancellable cancelled before / during / after the call, cancellable reset and reused, 500 concurrent loads cancelled in one shot (all 500 rejected in 19 ms, no hang), 200 in-flight operations whose File and Cancellable are unreachable from JS with 20 forced major GCs. Rejections carry domain, code and message; `error instanceof Gio.IOErrorEnum` and `error.code === Gio.IOErrorEnum.CANCELLED` both work. No hangs, no criticals.
- quit(): with async work pending, twice in a row, from inside a signal handler, from inside a signal handler twice. All exit 0 cleanly.
- GLib sources: idleAdd, timeoutAdd, a source removed from inside its own callback (works), a source removed after it already fired, a source removed twice.
- Signals: same handler connected twice, disconnect during emission, block/unblock via GObject.signalHandlerBlock/Unblock, 20000 connect/disconnect cycles, onSignal/offSignal/onceSignal (offSignal is correctly idempotent), disconnect of a stale id, disconnect of a never-issued id, connect and emit of a signal that does not exist (both throw a clean JS error).
- Throws and rejections: a throw from a signal handler (propagates to the emit caller), an unhandled rejection from a signal handler and from a React effect, a throw from a GLib timeout callback (becomes an uncaughtException, the source is removed, the loop stays healthy).
- Hooks outside context: useApplication outside GtkApplication throws "useApplication must be called within GtkApplication"; useParentWindow returns null outside a window and null-then-object inside one, exactly as its JSDoc says.
- Signals to the process: SIGINT 130, SIGTERM 143, SIGHUP 129, no criticals — Node defaults, not defects.
- Leak: 2000 mount/unmount cycles of a 120-widget tree. RSS climbs 185 -> 341 MB over the first 600 cycles then plateaus flat to cycle 2000. No leak.
- Roots: unmount twice (clean), a second createRoot on rootElement rendering a second GtkApplication (prints "Failed to register: An object is already exported for the interface org.gtk.Application" and exits 1 — arguably correct, not reported).

Could not reach: real window-manager close (headless weston gives no titlebar, so `gtk_window_close()` was used, which GTK documents as the same path); ASan/Miri verification against the source worktree (the brief forbids writing there and I did not want to build it); `pnpm nx run @gtkx/e2e:test:asan`; GObject handle counts (no public API exposes one, so the leak check is RSS-only); GSettings-backed lifetime (belongs to `deploy`).

Not reported although reproducible 10/10: `GLib.Source.remove()` on a source that already returned SOURCE_REMOVE emits `GLib-CRITICAL: Source ID N was not found` and aborts under fatal-criticals. This is what a React cleanup naturally does with a one-shot timeout, but `g_source_remove` is a 1:1 binding of a C function whose own documentation warns about exactly this, so GTKX exposes it faithfully. Its sibling `GObject.disconnect` is a GTKX-authored override with its own JSDoc, which is why that one IS reported below.

confirmed.reasoning:
Confirmed. No rule-out holds.

Not sanctioned by the C API. GLib's own doc for the parameter (glib/gutf8.c:2229, reproduced verbatim in the generated JSDoc) defines `end` as "the first byte of the first invalid character ... or the end of the text being validated ... either the trailing nul byte, or the first byte beyond @max_len (if it's positive)". A one-past-the-end cursor bounded by max_len is not a NUL-terminated array and carries no promise of being dereferenceable. GTKX binds it as `t.array(t.uint8, "array", "borrowed")` and scans it for a terminator, so the documentation contradicts the binding rather than excusing it.

Not an API misuse. The generated signature is `utf8Validate(str: number[]) => [boolean, number[]]`; `[]` and `[0x61]` are well-formed, and nothing in the docs warns against them.

Not a machine or codegen artifact. PyGObject, on this machine against the same GLib and the same GIR, returns `(True, end=b'')` for both `b''` and `b'a'`, so the under-annotated GIR (`<array c:type="const gchar**"/>` with no zero-terminated and no length) is not fatal to a binding that marshals correctly. The defect is in the current worktree source, not only in the published 1.0.0 binary: `packages/codegen/src/gir/type-ref.ts:94` still defaults `isZeroTerminated` to true, `arrayExpression` still emits `tArray` for it, and the two Rust sites below are unchanged. It also reproduces through two independent encode paths: a plain JS array segfaults and leaks, while `new Uint8Array([0x61])` takes the `buffer_view_passthrough` path and still leaks 5/5, which excludes a single bad code path.

Not a duplicate. The ledger holds F001-F005 only (testkit user-event, AdwAlertDialog children, vitest worker strays); none concern marshalling.

Not a missing feature. The function is bound, typed, documented, and returns bytes GLib never produced.

Mechanism, established from the source and gdb rather than from the symptom. Under gdb the fault address is `si_addr = 0x1` and the faulting instruction is `cmpb $0x0,(%r8,%r9,1)` inside `native::ffi::codec::array::ArrayCodec::decode_null_terminated`, reached from `RefCodec::decode_with_context` and `native::api::call::call`. The crash is therefore in GTKX's own code, not in GLib. `0x1` is `Vec::as_mut_ptr()` on an empty `Vec<u8>`: `impl From<Vec<$descriptor>> for StashStorage` (storage.rs:387) derives the FFI pointer straight from the vector, so an empty `str` argument reaches C as the dangling alignment pointer. `g_utf8_validate_len` with max_len 0 writes that pointer back through `end`, the null guards at ref.rs:220 and null_terminated.rs:158 do not fire because `0x1` is non-null, and `zero_terminated_len` (null_terminated.rs:42) walks from it with no bound. With `[0x61]` the same unbounded scan starts one byte past the buffer GTKX allocated and returns adjacent heap, which is the round-trip violation.
confirmed.likelyLocation: packages/codegen/src/analysis/descriptor-render.ts:693, in arrayExpression (root cause); the crash and the leak surface in packages/native/src/ffi/codec/array/null_terminated.rs:42 zero_terminated_len and packages/native/src/ffi/stash/storage.rs:387 impl From<Vec<$descriptor>> for StashStorage
confirmed.suggestedFix: The classification is the root and should be fixed in `arrayExpression`. That function already degrades an array it cannot measure to `tUint64` through `hasUnknownArrayLength`, but the predicate fires only when GIR explicitly writes `zero-terminated="0"`. The zero-terminated layout is sound only when the callee allocates and terminates the buffer, which is exactly what transfer full or container conveys; for a transfer-none out array carrying neither `length` nor `fixed-size`, the callee returns a borrowed cursor into memory the caller owns and promises no terminator, so `arrayExpression` must stop emitting `tArray` for that combination and treat the extent as unstated. For `g_utf8_validate` and `g_utf8_validate_len` the useful surface is the offset `end - str`, which GTKX can compute because it already passes `str` and its length, and `packages/codegen/overrides/` is the established route for reshaping a small set of callables this way. Two Rust fixes belong alongside it because they are unsound independent of any GIR annotation: `impl From<Vec<$descriptor>> for StashStorage` must yield a null pointer when the vector is empty instead of `Vec::as_mut_ptr()`'s dangling value, since it currently hands every C callee `0x1` for any empty borrowed scalar array and is what converts the out-of-bounds read into a segfault; and `zero_terminated_len` must be unreachable for a pointer whose allocation GTKX does not own, so that a mis-annotated descriptor degrades into an error rather than an unbounded walk through the heap.

1. `packages/native/src/value/wrapper.rs` implements the GJS/PyGObject toggle-reference protocol: `install` (line 123) puts an `Rc<WrapperHandle>` in the object's qdata and calls `g_object_add_toggle_ref`; `on_toggle_notify`/`apply_wrapper_level` flip the napi reference between strong and weak as the GObject's refcount crosses 1.

Its body runs in this order: `handle.generation.set(0)`, remove from LIVE_TOGGLE_REFS, **`steal_qdata`** (the wrapper record is now gone), `delete_reference`, then **`g_object_remove_toggle_ref`**. Then make `tracked_gobject_value` consult that marker: for an object inside its own teardown, skip `acquire_decoded_ref` entirely and produce a `Handle::from_glib_borrow`, a handle that neither refs nor unrefs, and hand it to JS. The JS half needs the matching branch: `getOrCreateWrapper` must build the wrapper for a borrowed handle with `wrapHandle(handle, cls)` and must not call `registerWrapper`/`setWrapper`, so no napi reference and no second toggle reference are installed. The result is that the receiver of `dispose` and `finalize` is a call-scoped wrapper that leaves the reference count untouched, which is exactly GObject's contract for those slots (the receiver is not valid past the call unless the implementation takes its own reference), so `g_object_unref` finds the count still at 1 after dispose returns, proceeds to finalize, and frees the instance. Confirmed, and it is GTKX code, not GTK. None of the rule-outs hold. (1) Not GTK/Adwaita/GLib: the defect is entirely in the Node-side dev runner, reproduced in a bare Vite 8.2.1 project under /tmp with no GTK, no widgets, no compositor and no codegen store, so it is also not a machine artifact. (2) Not documented API misuse: website/guide/getting-started.md:61 states the opposite contract, "saving a component patches it into the window that is already open", and nothing in the CLI or docs warns about save frequency. There is no user-facing knob either: DevWatch in packages/cli/src/dev/supervisor.ts:19 covers config-file watching, not Vite's chokidar options. (3) Not a duplicate: findings.jsonl holds only F001-F005 (testing user-event, AdwAlertDialog children, vitest/weston strays). (4) Not a missing feature: the runner prints "Fast Refresh complete" and leaves the app permanently on a superseded revision, i.e. it reports success for work it dropped.

My isolated harnesses show the report's mechanism is only half right, and the correction matters for the fix. Two independent paths produce the symptom. Path A, dominant below ~50 ms: the watcher coalesces a burst into a single change event (measured 2 writes -> 1 event at 5/10/20 ms, 2 events at 50/120 ms, matching the reporter's characterize.txt threshold precisely). handleFileChange reacts to that single event by eagerly invalidating and calling ssrLoadModule, capturing whatever is on disk at that microsecond; the final write of the burst lands after the load and emits no further event, so nothing ever re-reads it (harness: loaded MARKER 1 at t=524, WRITE 2 at t=529, ssrLoadModule at t=3782 still MARKER 1). Path B, with two genuinely separate events: the later handler never issues its own fetch at all. Vite's module runner dedupes by URL in concurrentModuleNodePromises (vite/dist/node/module-runner.js:1181, cachedModule) with no invalidation check, and cachedRequest then returns the already-set mod.promise, so the second event resolves to the OLDER module rather than the newer one winning as the report claims (harness with a 400 ms transform: E1 and E2 both commit MARKER 1 while disk is MARKER 2).

Both paths trace to the same two lines of GTKX code: onFileChange fires `void reloadChangedFile(server, deps, changedPath)` per event with no queue and no coalescing, and handleFileChange treats the result of a single ssrLoadModule as authoritative with no re-check that the revision it loaded is still the revision on disk before calling deps.performRefresh() and logging completion.
confirmed.suggestedFix: The fix belongs in packages/cli/src/dev/runner.ts and needs both halves, because debouncing alone leaves path B and serialising alone leaves path A. Replace the fire-and-forget `void reloadChangedFile(...)` in onFileChange with a single-flight queue: keep a set of dirty paths and one running promise chain so at most one handleFileChange executes at a time and a burst of events for the same path collapses to one pass, which removes the concurrent ssrLoadModule calls that Vite's runner-level concurrentModuleNodePromises dedupe silently answers with a stale module. Then make handleFileChange verify what it actually loaded: capture a freshness token before the load (the environment module node's lastInvalidationTimestamp, or the file's mtimeMs plus size, or a content hash), and after `await server.ssrLoadModule(changedPath)` re-read that token; if it moved, the exports in hand are superseded, so discard them, re-invalidate and loop rather than calling deps.performRefresh() and logging "Fast Refresh complete". Only commit and log once the loaded revision matches the file on disk, and surface a warning if the loop hits a retry bound instead of silently succeeding. Complement this in createDevServerConfig (packages/cli/src/dev/vite-dev-server.ts) with `server: { middlewareMode: true, watch: { awaitWriteFinish: { stabilityThreshold: ~40ms, pollInterval: ~10ms } } }` so an editor's format-then-write or an atomic rename emits one event after the file settles, which is what makes the common single-save case correct rather than merely eventually correct. Cover it with a test in packages/cli/tests/dev/runner.test.ts that drives two change events for one path against a deps stub whose ssrLoadModule resolves out of order, and asserts the last-written revision is the one handed to performRefresh.

rejected.title: Every gtkx subcommand silently accepts unknown options, so a misspelled option yields a wrong artifact or a silent no-op with exit 0
rejected.why:
Ruled out as a missing feature rather than a broken one, and as third-party parser default behavior that no GTKX code path contradicts.

What the source does: /home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/packages/cli/src/cli.ts builds the command tree with citty (defineCommand + runMain, citty ^0.2.2) and each subcommand (packages/cli/src/commands/{build,codegen,docs,dev}.ts) declares only its own `args`. citty's parser (/home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/node_modules/.pnpm/citty@0.2.2/node_modules/citty/dist/index.mjs, `parseRawArgs`) calls node:util `parseArgs` with `strict: false` and never compares parsed keys against the declared argsDef. citty 0.2.2 contains no unknown-key check and exposes no strict mode that GTKX declined to enable. The asymmetry the report cites is citty's own: `runCommand` throws "Unknown command <name>" at line 216 of that same file, while option parsing has no equivalent branch.

Verified independently of the hunter's shell script and of this machine by driving citty's `parseArgs` against the exact argsDef the build command declares: `--asset-bse=../share/x` -> {}, `--nope` -> {}, `--cwd` -> {cwd: ""} (empty string, which resolveCwd in packages/cli/src/internal/entry-arg.ts treats as absent via `args.cwd ? resolve(args.cwd) : process.cwd()`), and `--asset-bse ../share/x` -> the value lands on the `entry` positional. The observations are parser-level, not a build artifact, not a stale store, not the compositor.

Why that is not a GTKX defect: every declared option behaves as documented, and every invocation in the report is one the CLI never advertised. `gtkx build --asset-bse=...` is semantically `gtkx build` with no asset base, and that is documented to emit `new URL(..., import.meta.url)` relative to dist/bundle.js. `gtkx codegen --forse` is semantically `gtkx codegen`, whose documented non-forced path is the fingerprint freshness check described in CLAUDE.md; `--force` still works and still repairs the store. No GTKX function computes a wrong value, drops a value it received, or claims success for work it failed to do: it reports success for the work it was actually asked to do. Nothing in the CLI help, website/guide, or the API reference promises rejection of unknown options. The request is for a new validation layer (strict argument parsing) the CLI has never had, which is an absent hardening feature, not broken behavior. Not a duplicate either: findings.jsonl holds F001-F005, covering @gtkx/testing, @gtkx/react/adw, and @gtkx/vitest, none touching the CLI.

The one place the leniency shades toward wrong rather than merely permissive is `--cwd` with no value producing "", since citty coerces a valueless string option to the empty string and resolveCwd then falls back to process.cwd(). Even there the outcome equals the documented default of that option.

rejected.title: The string codec accepts null and undefined for a non-nullable `const gchar *` parameter and passes NULL to C, aborting the process on the resulting GLib assertion
rejected.why:
Ruled out on two of the listed grounds: (a) the reproduction misuses the API in a way GTKX's own documented contract forbids, and (b) what is missing is a feature (runtime nullability metadata) that the descriptor model has never had, not a codec that is broken.

1. GTKX does encode GLib's nullability contract, and it encodes it correctly. In the generated store the two cases are distinguished exactly as the GIR annotations say: `/home/eugenio/gtkx-playground/marshal-r1/node_modules/.gtkx/gi/glib/glib.d.ts:23771` declares `pathGetBasename(fileName: string): string`, while `.../gi/gtk/gtk.d.ts:10486` declares `setTooltipText(text: string | null): void`. `packages/codegen/src/gir/parameter.ts:99` reads `nullable` / `allow-none` off the GIR node, and `packages/codegen/src/gir/nullable-overrides.ts` even patches libraries that under-annotate. `website/guide/configuration-and-codegen.md:124` presents the generated `string | null | undefined` typing as the surface users program against. So the declared, documented contract for `g_path_get_basename` is non-nullable, and the repro is a hand-written `.mjs` that exists specifically to get past `tsc`. Oracle 6 (passes tsc, then blows up) does not fire: `GLib.pathGetBasename(null)` is a compile error. That is the "app code is provably misusing GTK" carve-out in oracle 2, and it is provable statically, from GTKX's own typings.

2. Mapping JS nullish to the C zero value is a deliberate, system-wide convention, not a hole in the string codec. `packages/native/src/ffi/codec/string.rs:18` (`read_string`) returns `None` for Null/Undefined, and every sibling codec does the same thing: `unichar.rs:47` (nullish to 0), `numeric.rs:264` (0.0), `bigint.rs:61` (0), `array.rs:96`, `buffer.rs:32`, `hashtable.rs:261`, `ref.rs:51`, `callback.rs:68`, and `value.rs:27` all map nullish to NULL/0. That convention is what makes `setTooltipText(null)`, `transientFor={null}`, `FileDialog.open(parent, null)` and `setError(null)` work, all of which the guides teach (`website/guide/async-operations.md:16`, `modals-and-portals.md:52`, `opengl.md:166`).

3. The runtime physically cannot tell the two cases apart, because nullability is never plumbed into the descriptor. `StringDescriptor` in `packages/runtime/src/descriptors.ts:179` is `{ kind, ownership, length? }`; there is no nullability field on any descriptor, and no occurrence of "nullable" anywhere under `packages/runtime/src` or `packages/native/src`. The emitted descriptors for the non-nullable and the nullable case are byte-identical: `t.fn(..., "g_path_get_basename", { args: [{ type: t.string("borrowed") }] ... })` versus `t.fn(..., "gtk_widget_set_tooltip_text", { args: [..., { type: t.string("borrowed") }] ... })`. `nullable` is consumed only by the TypeScript renderer (`packages/codegen/src/store/gi/method.ts:110,665`). Enforcing it at runtime means adding a new per-parameter metadata channel through codegen, the descriptor model, the N-API bridge and every codec: a feature request, which the brief excludes.

4. The report's asymmetry argument does not hold. The interior-NUL check (`string.rs:9`) exists because an interior NUL is not representable as a C string at all; a JS `null` is perfectly representable as a NULL pointer and is the required encoding for the thousands of `(nullable)` string parameters. The two are not comparable inputs.

5. What GLib does here is its documented behavior for a violated precondition. `g_return_val_if_fail` logs a CRITICAL and returns the default value; that is GLib's programmer-error mechanism, not a fault of the caller-side binding. With `G_DEBUG` unset, `g_variant_new_string` returns NULL and GTKX faithfully decodes NULL as `null`, so the report's "returns garbage" is inaccurate: `variant=null` is the correct marshalling of the NULL GLib returned, and the follow-on `TypeError: Cannot read properties of null` is ordinary JS. The abort is produced by `G_DEBUG=fatal-criticals`, a GLib debug switch the brief itself sets; GTKX neither sets it in user apps nor chooses to abort.

I confirmed the repro is not a machine artifact (`variantNewString` and `pathGetBasename` both exit 134 with the quoted critical) and it is not in the ledger: `/home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/.bughunt/findings.jsonl` holds F001-F005, covering user-event selection/expander/sort, AdwAlertDialog children, and leaked vitest workers. Nothing about marshalling.

rejected.title: The integer, float and enum codecs silently coerce null and undefined to 0 instead of rejecting them
rejected.why:
Reproduced (10/10) and traced to a deliberate branch, but GTKX is not at fault. Three points rule it out.

1. The nullish -> 0 branch is required by the published typed surface, so it cannot be removed. `coerce_number` (packages/native/src/ffi/codec/numeric.rs:256-267) maps `ValueType::Null | ValueType::Undefined` to `0.0`. Codegen maps `gpointer`/`gconstpointer` to the primitive category `pointer` (packages/codegen/src/gir/primitives.ts:91-92), whose TS type is `number` (line 113) and whose descriptor is a plain integer codec: the generated `gtk_buildable_parse_context_push` binding is `args: [struct, struct, t.uint64]`, and its declaration is `push(parser: BuildableParser, userData: number | null)`. The same pattern covers `GObject.Object.setData(key: string, data: number | null)`, every `Closure.marshal*(..., invocationHint: number | null, marshalData: number | null)`, and `Gsk.Stroke.equal(stroke1: number | null, stroke2: number | null)`. Those calls are TypeScript-clean and depend on null marshalling to a NULL pointer. Verified at runtime in the hunter's own playground: `info.setData("k", null)` then `getData("k")` returns 0, `setData("k", 42)` returns 42. `IntegerCodec::U64` is what a `gpointer` slot and a `guint64` slot both encode through, with nothing in the descriptor to tell them apart, so rejecting nullish in the integer codec would break the declared nullable-pointer surface.

2. The second consumer is record construction. `renderRecordConstructorPropsInterface` renders every writable field prop unconditionally nullable (packages/codegen/src/store/gi/record-constructor.ts:39, `renderTsType(context, entry.field.type, true)`), so `new Cairo.RectangleInt({ x: null })` and `new Cairo.Glyph({ x: null })` (a double field, so no pointer story) typecheck today and must land as 0. `Encoder::encode` and `PtrWriter::write_value_to_ptr` in the `impl_numeric_codecs!` macro both route through the same `number_from_value`, so the argument path and the struct-field path cannot be separated at that layer either.

3. The premise "no caller can be relying on null meaning zero" is true, but the corollary "this is the one failure mode the user cannot detect" is false. The shipped declarations are `static newInt32(value: number)`, `setSize(size: bigint)`, `setFileType(type: FileType)`. I compiled the three reported calls under the playground's `strict` tsconfig with the installed 1.0.0 stores and got TS2345 on all three ("Argument of type 'null' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number' / 'bigint' / 'FileType'"), while `push(parser, null)` compiled clean. The failure is caught at compile time, earlier than a throw. The contrast rows the report leans on are the opposite case: 1.5, NaN, -1 and 9999 are all `number`-typed, so range and integrality are exactly what the type system cannot express and what the codec is there to catch. Nullish for a non-nullable numeric parameter is what the type system already catches, and it is meaningful in the slots where the typings do admit it. That boundary is coherent, deliberate, and pinned by `integer_encode_accepts_number_object_and_optional_null` (packages/native/tests/numeric_codec.rs:216-244). What is left of the report is a request to also harden against callers who bypass the typings, i.e. a missing capability rather than a broken one.

Not a duplicate of F001-F005, and not a machine artifact: the branch is in the checked-in source and the behavior follows from it.

Reproduced 3/3 failures, then ruled the report out on two independent grounds.

(1) The probe assertion (the report's own stated root cause) asks for values GTK4 documents as unreachable. Gtk-4.0.gir: `gtk_event_controller_get_current_event` "Returns the event that is currently being handled by the controller. At other times, %NULL is returned"; `gtk_event_controller_get_current_event_state` "Returns the modifier state of the event that is currently being handled by the controller. At other times, 0 is returned"; `gtk_gesture_single_get_current_button` "Returns the button number currently interacting with @gesture, or 0 if there is none". Emitting `pressed` on a GtkGestureClick (packages/testing/src/user-event/click.ts:emitGesture) is signal emission, not `gtk_event_controller_handle_event`, so NULL/0/0 is the correct GTK4 answer. GTK4 also removed public GdkEvent construction: `<class name="ButtonEvent">` in /usr/share/gir-1.0/Gdk-4.0.gir carries exactly one member, `get_button`, and no constructor, so no off-screen harness can put an event behind the gesture through public API. GTKX already states this in the `click` JSDoc: "a gesture it attached itself, reading a GdkEvent that off-screen synthesis cannot produce." Control test confirmed it is universal, not click-specific: `userEvent.pointer(target, "[MouseLeft>]")` and `userEvent.dblClick(target)` both leave the probe at `state=0 button=0 event=false`. That is GTKX faithfully exposing a GTK4 limitation.

(2) Modifier-aware clicking is an absent capability, not a broken one. `createInstance` (packages/testing/src/user-event/index.ts) wires `click: after(click)` with no `state` argument, and `click`/`dblClick`/`tripleClick`/`pointer` take no modifier parameter anywhere in their signatures. No documentation claims otherwise: the `click` JSDoc is an exhaustive specification of the click outcome (button, indexed child, native row, tree expander, column header, cell transparency) and never mentions modifiers; the guide's off-screen limitations sentence covers `pointer` being left-button-only and `drag` refusing a Gtk.Range. The `setup` sentence the report cites, "held modifiers and buttons carry across its calls", is satisfied as written and is exercised by packages/testing/tests/user-event.test.tsx:359 ("retains a held modifier across calls until it is released", keyboard-to-keyboard `<Shift>F5`) and by `state.isMouseLeftDown` in pointer.ts: the state persists across calls, which is a different claim from click consuming it. The behavior observed under a held Control is precisely GTKX's documented plain-click outcome, calibrated deliberately in packages/e2e/tests/elements/row-click.test.tsx:577-609 ("replaces the selection across clicks…", "accumulates the selection when a single click also activates, as GTK does"); no test anywhere in the repo exercises a modifier-click. The multi-selection state the report wants is reachable through the documented helper: a control test with `userEvent.selectOptions(view, [0, 2])` then `[0, 1, 2]` on the same MULTIPLE ListView produced `sel=a,c` then `sel=a,b,c` and passed.

Also not a duplicate: F001/F002/F003 are plain-click outcomes not happening at all; here the plain click does select (`sel=c`). Not environmental: reproduced via three helpers and the positive control passes on the same display.

rejected.why:
Ruled out on three of the listed grounds: the GLib C API documents this behavior, the reproduction uses the raw API where GTKX documents and ships a guarded one, and what is being asked for is an added guard on a 1:1 binding rather than a broken function.

1. GLib documents the precondition and produces the message itself. `g_signal_handler_disconnect()` is documented as "Disconnects a handler from an instance ... The handler_id becomes invalid and may be reused." An already-invalid id violates the documented precondition, and GLib's own implementation reports it with `g_critical ("%s: instance '%p' has no handler with id '%lu'", G_STRLOC, ...)` after `handler_lookup()` misses. The observed text, including the source location `../gobject/gsignal.c:2723`, is GLib's own `G_STRLOC` string emitted inside libgobject; GTKX neither formats nor suppresses it. `GObject.prototype.disconnect` is a pure forwarding wrapper: `/home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/packages/codegen/overrides/gobject/object.ts.ejs` line 71 calls `disconnectSignal`, which at `/home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/packages/runtime/src/signal.ts:135-138` untracks and calls `gSignalHandlerDisconnect` bound from `g_signal_handler_disconnect`. That is faithful exposure of the C contract, exactly as GJS and PyGObject behave. The SIGABRT is not GTKX's either: `G_DEBUG=fatal-criticals` is GLib's documented debug switch whose entire purpose is to abort on the first `g_critical()`, so the reporter opted into turning GLib's designed diagnostic into a core dump.

2. GTKX documents and ships the idempotent path, and the reproduction bypassed it. `offSignal` (`/home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/packages/runtime/src/listeners.ts:103-118`) is the tracked surface, its JSDoc states "Does nothing if the handler is not currently connected," and it asks GLib via `isSignalHandlerConnected` before disconnecting, which is exactly why that check exists there and not on the raw id path. It is exposed as `off`/`removeEventListener` on every GObject. GTKX's own runtime and reconciler use only that path: `/home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/packages/react/src/reconciler/signals.ts` calls `target.object.off(...)` in `disconnectHandler` and `disconnectAllHandlers`, and raw `disconnect(id)` appears nowhere in GTKX's internals. The split is deliberate and covered: `/home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/packages/e2e/tests/runtime/listeners.test.ts:36-39` asserts `off()` after an earlier disconnect does not throw, while the `disconnect` describe block only covers a single live disconnect.

3. The dispose scenario the report offers as the "not by hand" variant is a tested, intentional contract, not an oversight. `/home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/packages/e2e/tests/runtime/disposed-listeners.test.ts` is a suite written specifically for it: "dispose destroys every handler, so each tracked id goes stale" asserts `signalHandlerIsConnected` returns false after `runDispose()`, and the remaining cases assert that `off()` after `runDispose()` or `GtkNativeDialog.destroy()` emits zero criticals. So GTKX already guarantees exactly what the report asks for, on the API meant for it, and the reproduction chose the unguarded one.

4. The symmetry argument does not hold. `connect`'s `Error: Unknown signal '...'` is not hand-added validation: it is the `default:` arm of the generated per-signal switch (`/home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/packages/codegen/src/store/gi/signal.ts:69-73`). `connect` must dispatch on the signal name to select the callback descriptor, so an unknown name has no code path to take and throwing is the only option. `disconnect` receives an opaque `gulong` with no dispatch; the only way to validate it is to ask GLib, which is precisely the guard GTKX placed on the tracked API.

Not a duplicate: findings.jsonl holds F001-F003 (`@gtkx/testing` user-event), F004 (`AdwAlertDialog` children), F005 (stray vitest workers), none of which touch signal disconnection. Not a machine artifact either, the behavior is deterministic libgobject code, but that does not matter given the above.

rejected.title: An application whose last window is closed or unmounted never exits, and the surviving invisible process makes every later launch of the same application exit silently with status 0
rejected.why:
Ruled out on three of the listed grounds: the GLib/GTK4 documentation says this is what happens outside `g_application_run()`, the GTKX documentation prescribes the explicit path the repro departs from, and the auto-quit was never implemented (a missing feature, not a broken one).

1. GLib locates the exit rule inside `g_application_run()`, which GTKX cannot enter. `Gio-2.0.gir`, `g_application_run`: "If, after the above is done, the use count of the application is zero then the exit status is returned immediately. If the use count is non-zero then the default main context is iterated until the use count falls to zero, at which point 0 is returned... Much like g_main_loop_run(), this function will acquire the main context for the duration that the application is running." `g_application_release`: "When the use count reaches zero, the application will stop running." `gtk_application_add_window`: "GTK will keep the application running as long as it has any windows"; `gtk_application_remove_window`: "The application may stop running as a result of a call to this function, if the window was the last window of the application." The termination is not an effect of removing the window; it is `g_application_run()`'s main-context iteration ending. GTKX deliberately never enters that loop, and says so at /home/eugenio/gtkx-bughunt/packages/runtime/src/lifecycle.ts:110-113: "`g_application_run()` is not what starts the application, because it would drive its own main loop and freeze Node; only the local command line handling it delegates to runs here." With nothing iterating inside `g_application_run`, a use count of zero has no process-level meaning. Process lifetime instead belongs to Node's loop, held by `keepAlive(true)` (lifecycle.ts:82, 142) and released by `keepAlive(false)` on the application's `shutdown` signal (lifecycle.ts:85-87); `packages/native/src/api/keep_alive.rs` documents it as "keeping the Node event loop alive". This is GApplication behaving as documented when embedded in a foreign main loop.

2. The two GTKX statements the report cites as promises do not say what it claims. The `runApplication` JSDoc sentence "{@link quitApplication} calls it once no window holds the application open, to reach the teardown only it performs" has "it" bound to `g_application_run()` from the previous sentence, and describes `quitApplication`'s own sequence: lifecycle.ts:164-168 detaches every window first, then line 170 calls `shutDownThroughRun`, precisely so `run()` returns immediately instead of iterating a main loop. It is a description of why the windows are removed before the call, not a claim that anything invokes `quitApplication` when the window set empties. `website/guide/modals-and-portals.md`'s "A window element presents itself on mount and destroys the window on unmount" is implemented and true (`destroyWindow` in packages/react/src/components/window.tsx:19-23, and `application.removeWindow(window)` in packages/react/src/element-behaviors.ts:308); it says nothing about the process.

3. What GTKX does document is the opposite of the report's expectation. website/tutorial/your-first-window.md:94: "Here it calls `quit()` to end the process when you close the last window." website/guide/getting-started.md:94: "Shutting down is the mirror image. `quit()` from `@gtkx/react` unmounts every root, and unmounting the application element quits the application it started... so the starter hands it to its main window as `onCloseRequest={quit}`." The scaffolded starter emits it (packages/create-gtkx/src/templates/src/app.tsx.ejs:14) and every shipped example wires it (examples/hello-world/src/app.tsx:10, examples/browser/src/app.tsx:144, examples/gtk-demo/src/app.tsx:480, examples/tutorial/src/components/window.tsx:64). The repro instead keeps `<GtkApplication>` mounted with zero windows and expects an implicit exit, which is the documented responsibility of the application author. The documented path works and is exercised: e2e keep-alive tests assert `keepAlive(false)` follows `quitApplication`, and `quit()` unmounts every root (packages/react/src/reconciler/root.ts:140-146), whose application-element cleanup calls `quitApplication` (packages/react/src/components/application.tsx:52-55).

4. Not a regression and not a half-built path: `git log -S"window-removed" --all -- packages/` returns nothing, so no window-set watcher ever existed to break. A windowless registered application is a state GTKX supports on purpose, covered by the `--gapplication-service` case in packages/e2e/tests/runtime/keep-alive.test.ts:27-39 ("holds the loop for a registered application that never activated").

5. The second half is plain GApplication single-instance behavior, not a distinct GTKX behavior. `g_application_run`'s documentation describes the non-primary process forwarding its command line and returning immediately; any GTK application still running makes the next launch a remote instance that exits 0. It follows from the first half rather than standing on its own.

6. An eager `window-removed` quit would also break correct programs: React commits deletions before placements in a single mutation pass, so an application that swaps window A for window B in one commit transiently holds zero windows and would exit. GLib tolerates the same transient only because the run loop defers; a direct signal handler would not.

rejected.title: GLib timeouts, idles and promisified GIO calls never run when no application element is mounted: the process exits 0 immediately and the awaited promise never settles
rejected.why:
Ruled out on two grounds: the GLib C API documents this exact behavior, and the part that is not GLib semantics is a convenience GTKX never claimed, not a broken path.

1. GLib's model. A GSource does nothing on its own: it dispatches only while some thread iterates the GMainContext it is attached to (GMainContext docs; g_timeout_add_full attaches to the default context and is dispatched by whoever iterates it). Nothing in GLib makes a pending source extend a process's life. This holds inside GApplication too: g_application_run() returns when the use count drops to zero, and the use count is raised by g_application_hold(), attached windows and running actions, never by a pending timeout. So the report's stated expectation, "the pending GLib source keeps the process alive until it runs, the way a Node timer does", is not GLib behavior in any GLib program. A C or GJS equivalent (g_timeout_add without g_main_loop_run) prints nothing and exits 0 identically.

2. GTKX mirrors that model faithfully, and the integration is not asleep. packages/native/src/runloop.rs installs a uv_prepare handle whose callback (on_prepare, line 293) drives g_main_context_iteration on every libuv turn, then arms a uv timer/pollers for the next GLib wakeup. Both handles are uv_unref'd at install (lines 364-367) so GLib alone never pins the Node loop; set_keep_alive (line 407) uv_ref's the prepare handle, and packages/runtime/src/lifecycle.ts calls keepAlive(true) on registration/activate and keepAlive(false) on shutdown. That is GApplication's hold/release count expressed in libuv terms, which is precisely the C model.

3. The report's claim about idles is factually wrong, which pins the mechanism as "not yet ready when the loop drained", not "dropped". A probe I built and ran in the same directory (src/probe-idle-check.ts -> "[idle-check] idle fired", exit 0) shows a source that is ready on the first prepare pass dispatches before the process exits. Only work whose deadline lies past the drain point is left unrun, exactly as GLib specifies.

4. There is a supported route, and it is GLib's own. src/probe-mainloop-check.ts (GLib.MainLoop.new(null,false) + loop.run()) prints "timeout fired at 200ms" and exits 0; src/probe-mainloop-async.ts resolves loadContentsAsync the same way. GLib.MainLoop is in the generated @gtkx/gi/glib surface, and @gtkx/runtime additionally exports createApplication + runApplication publicly. A script has both the GLib primitive and the GApplication one available; neither is missing.

5. Auto-holding on pending sources, the report's proposed alternative, cannot be implemented: once Gtk.init runs, GTK and GDK keep permanently attached sources (frame clock, D-Bus, settings portal) on the default context, so ref'ing the prepare handle whenever sources exist would make every GTKX process hang forever instead of exiting.

Not a duplicate: F001-F005 in .bughunt/findings.jsonl cover @gtkx/testing user-event, AdwAlertDialog children and leaked vitest workers. Not a machine artifact either: it reproduces, and the same operation done the GLib way on the same machine works.

The residue is documentation-only. website/guide/async-operations.md says "GIO async methods return promises, so you await them like any other promise" and every example sits inside a component under a mounted application; a sentence stating that the GLib context is driven while the application holds the loop, and that a standalone script must run a GLib.MainLoop or a GApplication, would close the gap. That is a docs addition, not a runtime defect.
